blocks.text: Scenario A — Counselling
A 30-year-old woman attends your clinic and asks about cervical cancer screening. Explain the purpose, benefits, limitations and procedure.
Scenario B — Procedure
Demonstrate how you would obtain a cervical screening sample from an eligible patient.
Scenario C — Result interpretation
A patient's screening result shows high-risk HPV positivity with no cytological abnormality. Explain the result and the next steps.
Scenario D — Anxiety about HPV
A woman is worried that a positive HPV test means she has cancer or that her partner has been unfaithful. Counsel her.
Scenario E — Screening versus diagnosis
A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent postcoital bleeding. Should you perform routine cervical screening or arrange diagnostic assessment?
Cervical screening is the systematic testing of an eligible, generally asymptomatic population to identify high-risk HPV infection or cervical cellular abnormalities that may precede invasive cancer.

items.text: Detect high-risk HPV infection.
Identify precancerous cervical lesions.
Arrange further assessment and treatment before invasive cancer develops.
Reduce cervical cancer incidence and mortality.
Identify women who require closer follow-up or colposcopy.

blocks.text: Screening is most effective when it is part of an organised programme with reliable sample collection, laboratory processing, communication of results, follow-up and treatment.
There are three important approaches to know.
A. High-risk HPV testing
Detects genetic material from oncogenic HPV types.
Often the preferred primary screening method in modern screening programmes because persistent high-risk HPV infection is the major cause of cervical cancer.
B. Cervical cytology (Pap test)
Examines cervical cells for abnormalities such as ASC-US, LSIL and HSIL.
May be used as a primary screening method or as triage following a positive HPV test, depending on the programme.
C. Visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA)
The cervix is inspected after applying dilute acetic acid. Certain abnormal areas become acetowhite.
A visual screening approach used in some resource-limited settings. A positive result requires appropriate assessment and management under the local protocol.

blocks.text: The appropriate starting age, stopping age, screening interval and preferred method depend on national guidance, HIV status, previous screening results and prior cervical disease.
For OSCE purposes, distinguish international guidance from a specific national programme.

items.text: The World Health Organization recommends HPV DNA testing as the preferred primary screening method where feasible, generally beginning at age 30 in the general population and using defined intervals.
WHO recommends an earlier starting age for women living with HIV, generally age 25, with shorter intervals.
Other programmes, including those in the UK and other high-income countries, use their own age ranges and testing schedules.
Previous high-grade lesions, cervical cancer, immunosuppression or other high-risk circumstances may require individualised surveillance rather than routine population screening.

blocks.text: Exam tip: If asked for a precise screening age or interval, state the guideline you are following. Do not combine one country's starting age with another country's interval.

Screening is intended primarily for asymptomatic people with a cervix. A woman with symptoms needs diagnostic assessment even if she is younger than the routine screening age or recently had a negative screening result.
A good OSCE answer should cover informed consent, confidentiality, procedure, limitations and follow-up.

"Cervical screening checks for certain types of HPV or changes in cervical cells that could eventually lead to cervical cancer. It is designed to identify risk early, before cancer develops. It does not mean that you have cancer, and it cannot detect every cervical abnormality."

content_groups.group_title: B. Speculum examination and sample collection

items.text: Inspect the external genitalia as appropriate.
Gently insert a suitable speculum using the technique taught by your institution.
Visualise the cervix fully.
Assess whether the cervix looks suspicious. If it does, arrange diagnostic referral rather than treating screening as sufficient.
Collect the sample from the appropriate cervical area and transformation zone using the approved brush or sampling device.
Transfer or rinse the sample into the correct container according to the kit instructions.
Label the sample accurately and complete the request form.
Gently remove the speculum.
Offer the patient tissues and privacy to dress.
Explain the expected timeframe and how results will be communicated.

Common mistake: taking a sample without first confirming that the cervix has been adequately visualised and that the patient is attending for screening rather than evaluation of suspicious symptoms.

blocks.text: These are cytology categories, not cancer stages.

content_groups.group_title: How to interpret them in an OSCE

items.text: NILM: reassure appropriately, but manage any HPV result and screening history according to the programme.
ASC-US: low-grade or uncertain cellular changes; management depends on HPV status, age and prior results.
LSIL: commonly associated with HPV infection; follow-up or colposcopy depends on risk and the local protocol.
ASC-H: requires further assessment because high-grade disease cannot be excluded.
HSIL: requires prompt evaluation, usually colposcopy and biopsy or other management under the applicable pathway.
AGC: requires appropriate evaluation because glandular abnormalities may arise in the cervix or, depending on age and circumstances, elsewhere in the genital tract.
Unsatisfactory sample: repeat sampling or further assessment according to the guideline; do not interpret it as a negative result.

blocks.text: A cytology report alone cannot establish whether stromal invasion is present.
The result must be interpreted together with the screening history and local protocol.
Scenario 1
High-risk HPV negative
The risk of significant HPV-related cervical disease is low at that point.
Next step: return to the routine screening interval appropriate to the programme, unless symptoms or a history of significant disease require further assessment.
Scenario 2
High-risk HPV positive, cytology negative
HPV is present, but the sample has not shown cytological abnormalities.
Next step: follow the programme's risk-based pathway, which may include HPV genotyping, repeat HPV testing or colposcopy depending on the result and history.
Scenario 3
High-risk HPV positive with abnormal cytology
This increases concern for precancerous disease, especially with high-grade cytological changes.
Next step: arrange the appropriate triage and referral, often colposcopy and possible biopsy.
Scenario 4
Suspicious visible cervical lesion
This is no longer a routine screening question.
Next step: prompt specialist assessment and biopsy. A negative HPV test or cytology result should not delay investigation of a clinically suspicious lesion.

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Counselling a woman with a positive HPV test

blocks.text: This is a common communication station because patients may associate HPV with infidelity or cancer.

"Your test has detected a type of HPV that can be associated with cervical cell changes. HPV is extremely common and can remain undetected for months or years. A positive result does not mean that you have cervical cancer, and it cannot tell us when you acquired the infection or from whom.

Many HPV infections clear naturally. The important thing is that we follow the recommended pathway to check whether there are any cell changes that need treatment. I will explain what your particular result means and when you need your next test or referral."
Does HPV mean my partner has been unfaithful?
No. HPV can remain undetected for a long time, so the result cannot establish when the infection was acquired or prove infidelity.
Do I have cervical cancer?
Not necessarily. HPV positivity indicates infection with a virus associated with cervical cancer risk. Further testing determines whether cervical cell abnormalities are present.
Will HPV go away?
Many infections become undetectable through the body's immune response. Persistent high-risk infection requires appropriate follow-up.
Can I still become pregnant?

An HPV-positive result alone does not prevent pregnancy. Some treatments for significant cervical precancer can affect future pregnancy risks, so fertility wishes should be discussed before treatment.
Can vaccination help?
HPV vaccination prevents important new HPV infections, but it does not treat an existing infection or replace recommended screening.
This distinction is especially important in OSCEs.

blocks.text: Exam practice

A 32-year-old woman attends for routine cervical screening. Her result shows high-risk HPV positivity, but cytology is negative for intraepithelial lesion or malignancy. She asks whether she has cervical cancer.
What is the best response?
She definitely has cervical cancer and requires immediate chemotherapy.
The result means she has acquired HPV recently.
HPV has been detected, but no cytological abnormality was found; the next step depends on the screening pathway and her history.
No follow-up is needed because the cytology is negative.
